title: Buried with him (Romans 6:3–4)
hook: baptized into his death to walk in newness of life

segments.voice: Yesterday, love poured out before we deserved it. Your line was while we were yet sinners. Were you kind to someone before they earned it? Day five hundred sixty-three.

In some old churches, the baptismal font isn't a basin. It's a pool, set into the floor, with steps going down one side and up the other. Some are even shaped like a tomb, or a cross. You walk down into the water, you go under, and you come up the other side. Nobody designed that by accident. The shape is a sermon in stone, and the sermon comes from two verses in Romans 6.
screen: `A FONT WITH STEPS DOWN.` → `SHAPED LIKE A TOMB.` → `A SERMON IN STONE.`

segments.voice: Paul has just said that where sin abounded, grace abounded more. Someone might take that and say: great, then let's keep sinning so there's more grace. Paul's answer is, God forbid. And then he asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "Know you not that all we, who are baptized in Christ Jesus, are baptized in his death?" The Greek word baptizo means to dip or plunge, to immerse. Paul sees baptism as a plunge into Christ's own death and burial. Then verse four: "For we are buried together with him by baptism into death; that as Christ is risen from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we also may walk in newness of life." Buried with him. The old self goes down into the water the way a body goes into a grave. And just as Christ came up from the tomb, the baptized come up to walk, step by step, in a life that's new. Not a fresh coat of paint on the old life. A new one. It's why the Church baptizes new members at the Easter Vigil, the night between Christ's burial and his rising. It's why the newly baptized are handed a candle lit from the Easter candle. And it's why there are fonts with steps down and steps up. Whether a person is immersed in a pool or has water poured on the head, Catholics believe the same thing happens: dying and rising with Christ. Someone baptized as an infant doesn't remember it. Paul writes as though it shapes every step after: walk in newness of life.
screen: `SHALL WE SIN THAT GRACE MAY ABOUND?` · `BAPTIZO: TO PLUNGE.` · `BURIED WITH HIM.` · `RAISED UP, TO WALK.` · then, large: `NEWNESS OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless yourself with water. If you're near a church, holy water is by the door. If not, any water will do as a reminder: the kitchen tap, a glass, a bathroom sink. Settle, and breathe. Touch the water with your fingers. Catholics make the sign of the cross with it, remembering their baptism. If that's not your practice, just feel the cool of it and think of one old habit you'd like to leave in the water, and one step of new life you'd like to take today. Let the water dry on your skin. The bell holds the time.
Baptizo. The Greek word for plunge or immerse: Paul's picture of baptism as a burial with Christ, and a rising to newness of life. Today's word.
Your line: newness of life. Today, every time you wash your hands, remember one thing you've left behind. Day five hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics bless themselves with holy water as they enter a church, recalling their baptism, and Romans 6:3–11 is the Epistle read at the Easter Vigil, the night new members are baptized.

original.note: Greek: to dip, plunge or immerse. Paul hears in it a burial and a rising.

trapdoor: what you thought: baptism is a ceremony for babies with a little water.
what it means: Paul sees it as being buried with Christ and raised to walk in a new life.
what a scholar hears: baptizō means to plunge. some early fonts were built like tombs or crosses with steps down and up, and the Easter Vigil was the great night for baptism.

sources.quoted: Know you not that all we, who are baptized in Christ Jesus, are baptized in his death?
For we are buried together with him by baptism into death; that as Christ is risen from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we also may walk in newness of life.

notes: Romans 6:3–11 as the Epistle at the Easter Vigil: confirm.
Early cruciform and tomb-shaped fonts (e.g. at Shivta, Ephesus, Lechaion): confirm the general claim.
CCC 1214 (baptizein = plunge, burial and resurrection); CCC 1239 (immersion or pouring): confirm.
'Paschal candle given to the newly baptized': the baptismal candle is lit from the Paschal candle; the script says the candle lit from the Easter fire is given; confirm phrasing.

Editor review (2026-10-01): Romans 6:3–4 now quoted from the Douay-Rheims, not the KJV. Cut the 'most people were baptized as infants' statistic and the unsourced 'early Church baptized at the Vigil' claim; the baptismal candle is now lit from the Easter (Paschal) candle, not 'the Easter fire'. Douay wording checked against drbo.org.
